context.transcript_excerpt: Hello and welcome back to the Freight Flow Advisor Brief, the show where we break down the freight stories that actually affect cost, capacity, service, and overall decisions in the supply chain. Now, if you're a shipper or a carrier or a forwarder or a broker or even an operator trying to make sense of a volatile freight market, this podcast was designed for you. We like to cut through the headlines and explain what is changing and how it affects your network. Today, we're going to be talking about ocean containers and an uncomfortable development for shippers. Let's face it, rate pressure is moving from the spot market into contract rates. I recently had a conversation with Peter Tershwell, and he's one of the most experienced and respected voices in container shipping. Peter pointed me to his recent article titled A New Paradigm in Ocean Containers, and it sharpened a question I think the market needs to take seriously. We have spent a lot of time talking about the record order book. We know the conventional view. Too many ships should mean lower freight rates. But what if the more important number is not how many ships exist? What if it's how many ships are actually available? on the right trade lane, operating reliably enough to move cargo on time. Because right now, that effective capacity is being constrained by congestion, not to mention geopolitical disruption. And you put that together with carrier capacity management, and it creates this recipe. And that is why the market is behaving differently than the simple more ships equal cheaper freight. So let's start with the latest. According to Lodestar, Asia to Los Angeles spot rates rose 6% to $6,244 per 40-foot container. That alone will get attention, but the bigger signal is what happened alongside it. Average long-term rates on Asia to U.S. West Coast and East Coast trades were up 41% and 40% respectively. So if I were to put this in plain English, a spot rate is the price you would pay for a shipment moving now or very soon. It moves quickly with demand, available vessel space, port conditions, and carrier pricing. Conversely, a contract rate is supposed to provide more stability. A shipper commits volume, the carrier commits capacity, and a rate structure. Both sides get more predictability. Now, typically, a spot rate will move first. while contract rates move more slowly, and sometimes they do not follow spot rates at all. And that lag is important. It gives shippers time to assess whether a spike is temporary or structural. But when the spot market pressure starts to flow into contracts, the message is different. Carriers believe the disruption is durable enough to reprice longer-term commitments. And that's the simple point behind Lodestar's phrase, the, quote, rate increase fire is spreading from spot rates to contract rates. Now, my view of this after speaking with Peter is that shippers should not dismiss this as another headline driven spike, but they should not panic and lock in everything at elevated levels. The smarter response is to understand why capacity has become tight It also to figure out which costs are genuinely structural and where carriers may be using uncertainty to push pricing beyond the underlying economics Now are you ready for the paradox here? Peter's article highlights the scale of the vessel order book. By one estimate, he cites it's about 37% of the existing global fleet. That is enormous, and it is why analysts have been warning that container shipping could face a long period of overcapacity and weak carrier earnings. This analysis is not irrational. New ships do matter. Supply eventually matters and demand eventually matters. But in ocean freight, installed capacity is not the same thing as usable capacity. pending_qa.q: To what extent are carriers reducing scheduled capacity across major east-west trade lanes?
pending_qa.r: Carriers withdrew between 10 and 14 percent of scheduled capacity across four major east-west trades in the first half of 2026. Asia to U.S. East Coast had the highest withdrawal at 14 percent, followed by Asia to U.S. West Coast and Asia to North Europe at 11 percent each, and Asia to Mediterranean at 10 percent.

pending_qa.q: What recent rate movements signal that pressure is shifting from spot markets to contract rates?
pending_qa.r: According to Lodestar, Asia to Los Angeles spot rates rose 6% to $6,244 per 40-foot container. More significantly, average long-term rates on Asia to U.S. West Coast and East Coast trades were up 41% and 40% respectively, indicating carriers believe disruption is durable enough to reprice longer-term commitments.

pending_qa.q: How should freight operators evaluate carrier and forwarder performance beyond rate negotiations?
pending_qa.r: Shippers should separate rate risk from service risk by asking about actual schedule performance, what happens if a vessel skips the port, where empties come from, fallback gateway options, and how surcharges are governed. Missing sailings, late transshipments, poor equipment cycles, and delayed inland handoffs can be more expensive than rate increases and are often harder to see in time.

pending_qa.q: What contract provisions should address disruption in volatile ocean shipping environments?
pending_qa.r: Every significant ocean agreement should address routing changes, emergency surcharges, notice periods, force majeure, service failures, allocation treatment, and handling of cargo already in transit. Most contracts are written for normal conditions, but freight teams need them to work under abnormal conditions.

pending_qa.q: How do sourcing diversification decisions create logistics network exposure?
pending_qa.r: As companies diversify manufacturing beyond China to countries like Vietnam, Indonesia, Thailand, Cambodia, India, and Mexico, they reshape where freight risk sits. Diversifying sourcing without diversifying logistics creates new exposure, especially where congestion challenges and loading delays at developing Southeast Asian ports are material.
